frameworks.name: Two Windows of Buyer Readiness
frameworks.definition: Buyers fall into two distinct windows: immediate-pain buyers ready today, and long-term nurture buyers who become ready over 24-36 months as you stay present.

frameworks.name: Outbound as Long-Term Nurture Motion
frameworks.definition: Outbound sales seeds the market initially; most converts into long-term nurture (email, retargeting, content) that keeps the seller top-of-mind when the buyer's pain becomes urgent.

claims.text: In almost any market, 97% of buyers are not ready to purchase today but will become ready within the next 24-36 months (Alex Hormozi, MoreMozi outbound sales session). Most businesses fail to scale because they only compete for the 3% ready immediately, while larger brands win by having messaging and nurture systems for all 100% of prospects.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applicable to outbound sales across most market types
claims.mechanism: Big brands scale because they capture buyers across both windows (immediate and future-ready), whereas small businesses compete only for the immediate 3%, cannibalizing the same small buyer pool.
bounded_by: Assumes the seller has nurture infrastructure (email, content, retargeting) to maintain presence over months
Does not apply to impulse-purchase categories where most buyers are ready immediately

claims.text: Outbound sales transitions from direct-response (immediate call booking) into long-term nurture pipeline (email sequences, retargeting ads, content) because most contacts will not buy immediately but will need to stay top-of-mind until they become ready.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Immediate outreach captures the 3% ready today; nurture messaging reaches the 97% who will become ready later by maintaining presence and relevance.

claims.text: There are two distinct windows when buyers make purchases: (1) immediate pain-driven (urgent problem, immediate budget), (2) long-term nurture-driven (initially unready, but became ready over 12-24+ months of exposure to the seller's content and presence).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Buyers in window 1 respond to direct outreach; buyers in window 2 require prolonged nurture and top-of-mind positioning before they perceive pain or urgency.
bounded_by: In very short-cycle categories (under 30 days), window 1 dominates and window 2 may be negligible

claims.text: Most entrepreneurs underestimate the required commitment horizon for outbound sales effectiveness because they expect measurable results within 30-90 days, but sales cycles (especially long-tail nurture) require 6+ months of continuous effort before ROI is visible.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Early-stage outbound produces low immediate conversion because it plants seeds; the market needs time to mature. Withdrawing before 6 months prevents compound nurture benefits and leaves money on the table.
bounded_by: Does not apply to viral/self-serve product launches where word-of-mouth compounds faster
Assumes consistent execution quality (bad outbound remains bad at any timeline)

claims.text: Entrepreneurial decisions often require commitment despite incomplete information; you cannot know if a sales motion will work until you commit to it for the full cycle (often 6+ months), so the decision rule is first-principles-based: 'If we get in front of more of the type of person who buys our stuff, we will make more money.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: insufficient historical data to model sales curves
claims.mechanism: Perfect information is impossible; waiting for certainty is itself a decision (to not scale). Committing to a first-principles hypothesis (more quality prospects → more sales) is more productive than seeking data validation before launch.
bounded_by: Does not apply to contexts where prior data exists (mature product, historical LTV/CAC data)
Assumes the first-principles rule is sound (correct buyer avatar)

examples.text: Hormozi conducted a live poll at a speaking event asking attendees when they first heard of him. The distribution showed: ~3% within 90 days, increasing to ~6% within 6 months, ~12% within 12 months, ~33% within 2 years, and roughly 67% over 2+ years. This visually demonstrated that most audience members had been exposed to his content across a long tail (months to years) before deciding to engage or purchase.

A prospect enters an outbound sales funnel but doesn't respond to the initial pitch. Rather than being lost, they enter email nurture sequences and retargeting campaigns. Over the next 6-12 months, they see repeat content and touchpoints. When they eventually experience pain related to the problem (triggered by business growth, competitive pressure, or internal event), they remember the seller because of sustained presence—and they become a sales-ready lead from the nurture stream, not from a fresh outreach.

practices.text: Measure outbound effectiveness not by immediate response rate or month-1 sales, but by pipeline maturity over 6-month horizons. Track the split of sales coming from direct response (month 0-3) vs. long-tail nurture (month 3-6+).

Build integrated nurture infrastructure (email sequences, content cadence, retargeting setup) concurrently with outbound launch, so prospects who don't convert immediately are automatically fed into long-term nurture streams.

For long-sales-cycle offerings, commit to outbound + nurture for a minimum of 6 months before evaluating ROI, assuming first-principles logic: 'More quality prospects in front of us = more revenue eventually.' Do not withdraw earlier based on short-term metrics.
